 After historic blue wave, Mississippi governor calls for end to mail ballot grace period 
 By Jacob Knutson , Jen Rice 
 November 18, 2026 
 Prefer us on Google 
 to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.
 Mississippi Republican Gov. Tate Reeves responds to a reporter's question, Jan. 25, 2024, at the state Capitol in Jackson, Miss. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis, File)

 Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves (R) is asking lawmakers to eliminate the state’s five-day grace period for mail ballots — the latest development in the GOP’s years-long attack on mail voting rights. 
 Reeves included the request in the proposed state budget recommendations his office released Tuesday. 
 The assault on voting accommodations comes after a seismic midterm election that saw Mississippi send its first Black senator to Congress since Reconstruction. Hundreds of late-arriving ballots helped seal Democratic challenger Scott Colom’s victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

 Reeves’ recommendation calls for ending the state’s five-day grace period that allows election officials to count mail ballots that are received after Election Day. The policy comes from a pandemic-era expansion that made voting more accessible.
 Under his proposal, ballots would be thrown out if received after 5 p.m. on Election Day. 
 “COVID-19 is now a distant memory, and Mississippi election laws should be amended to reflect the history and tradition of American democracy,” Reeves wrote, failing to explain how the proposed change was related to the state budget.
 In Hinds County alone this year, 67 mail ballots arrived after Election Day and were processed on the same day the race was called for Colom.
 Mississippi is central to Republican attempts to eliminate protections for ballots that arrived after Election Day through no fault of the voters.
 A GOP challenge to the Magnolia State’s grace period for mail ballots led to the landmark Supreme Court decision * in Watson v. Republican National Committee (RNC). In its March 2026 ruling, the Court found that grace periods for certain ballots are constitutional, rejecting Republicans’ argument that all elections conclude on Election Day as defined by the U.S. Constitution.
 Reeves’ request also comes as Mississippi civil rights and voting groups hope this year’s historic election could lead to voting reforms that expand — not restrict — the right to vote.
 *Intervenors in Watson were represented by the Elias Law Group (ELG). ELG Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.
